verdict: Clean on the mechanical checks (no forbidden language, no em-dash outside the verbatim Whitehead and Perry quotation, the one exclamation is inside Luke 19:42, standfirst is one plain sentence, headings plain). The argument is his: fair to the patriot first, Augustine and Orwell doing real work, Amos as the diagnosis, an ending on the cross. What a careful reader still hears is a verdict-sentence habit: seven sentences open 'That is / That's', and a paragraph several times closes on a balanced 'X, not Y' line. The one first-person paragraph is a stub since its memory clause was cut, and the essay is cool throughout: there is no place where James is visibly in the room. Small trims fix the tics; only James can fix the last.

findings.quote: Amos told Israel that the covenant made them more accountable, not less.
findings.tell: Paragraph says its point three times; antithesis as habit
findings.why: The sentence states the conclusion before the verse, then two lines later 'The privilege didn't exempt Israel from judgment. It was the reason for the judgment.' says it again in a second antithesis. A person makes the point once, after the text.
findings.replacement: Amos told Israel what that covenant meant.

findings.quote: That is civil religion standing beneath God instead of beside Him.
findings.tell: Aphoristic balanced closer; the 'That is ...' verdict stamp (seven sentences in the essay open this way)
findings.why: A preposition-swap epigram at the paragraph end, the fourth 'That is' verdict by this point. It reads as a manufactured kicker where the Lincoln quotation has already landed.
findings.replacement: Lincoln's civil religion left the nation answerable to God.

findings.quote: This doesn't settle how a Christian should vote. It settles something prior, which is where the love of country sits.
findings.tell: 'It is not X. It is Y.' antithesis, second in the closing movement, followed by another balanced antithesis ending the same paragraph
findings.why: The paragraph opens on one antithesis and closes on another ('rather than one of the many places where He is served'). Two in five sentences is the tic VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md puts on the avoid list.
findings.replacement: How a Christian should vote is a separate question. The prior one is where the love of country sits.

findings.quote: I came to faith out of atheism. A Christianity that seems to exist to bless one country is easy to explain away as that country's mythology,
findings.tell: Biography left as a stub; reads as a credential drop
findings.why: The clause that tied the fact to the argument was cut at the final read, so the sentence now sits alone and the next sentence does not follow from it. A reader hears a biographical fact inserted because the rules ask for one.
findings.replacement: I came to faith out of atheism, and I know that a Christianity that seems to exist to bless one country is easy to explain away as that country's mythology,

findings.quote: Still, the sentence people remember tells us something. Faith was prized as a national asset,
findings.why: 'Tells us something' announces a point instead of making it; the brief lists vague framing sentences among the tells earlier judges caught.
findings.replacement: Still, in the sentence people remember, faith was prized as a national asset,

findings.quote: What the data describe is less a kind of devotion than a kind of belonging.
findings.tell: Balanced 'less a kind of X than a kind of Y' symmetry
findings.why: Perfectly parallel, and the next sentence makes the same point concretely. It is one more antithesis in a section that already has 'Christians taking part in civic life isn't fusion. Fusion is ...'.
findings.replacement: What the data describe is a kind of belonging.

findings.quote: A Christian can love America deeply and still know that the people of God are not Americans first.
findings.why: 'Deeply' adds heat without content; the sentence is stronger plain.
findings.replacement: A Christian can love America and still know that the people of God are not Americans first.

findings.quote: That's the place from which a Christian can love America well.
findings.tell: 'That is ...' verdict closer, seventh instance; echoes the section heading
findings.why: By the last section the 'That is / That's' paragraph-ender is audible as a pattern, and this one restates the heading above it.
findings.replacement: A Christian can love America well from there.

strengths: The patriot's case is given first and at full strength, in his own voice ('he'd go on', 'he'd say'), and conceded in one plain line: 'He is right about nearly all of that.'

Sources explain mechanisms rather than decorate: Augustine's ordered love, Orwell's distinction, Hall's objection to Whitehead and Perry, Bellah on Lincoln. Remove any name and the paragraph loses its idea.

'Jesus loved Jerusalem the way a Jew loves Jerusalem, and He would not let it stand in the place of God.' is the earned thesis line, and the ending returns to it and lands on the cross without a recap.
The 2 Chronicles 7:14 paragraph reads Scripture in context and turns the verse on the people praying it; the church is inside the diagnosis ('We haven't always remembered why').
Mechanically clean: no forbidden word, no em-dash in his own prose, no exclamation outside Scripture, contractions present, plain headings, one-sentence standfirst.
for_james: The essay has no moment where you are personally in it. 'I came to faith out of atheism' is the only first-person fact, and it has no memory attached (the earlier clause was cut because nobody could confirm it). If you actually remember how flag-and-cross Christianity looked to you as an unbeliever, one true sentence there would do more than any edit I can propose. I will not write it for you.

'it will cost something in this one' is true but unspecific. If there is a real cost you have paid or watched a pastor pay (a July service changed, a family that left), one concrete sentence would make the line yours. Only you can supply it.

'My own tradition ought to know better than most', followed by the Baptist history, tells the reader you are Baptist. That is a confirmed fact and no convention is named, but it is a statement of denomination by implication; confirm you want it.

The criticism of the left is one sentence with a link ('churches on the left can make a platform the measure of faithfulness'). On this subject unequal space is defensible, and your voice standard refuses false symmetry, but you should decide whether one sentence is enough.

Your saved Substack profile asks for 2 to 4 sentence paragraphs, 1,500 to 2,500 words, a Greek or Hebrew word, a 'screenshot' line and three Monday-morning questions with one practice. VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md asks for developed paragraphs and no application box, and this essay (about 3,300 words) follows it. I judged by VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md and did not rewrite toward the profile.
The only em-dashes in the piece are inside the verbatim Whitehead and Perry definition; they were left because the quotation is exact.
